Q1780180.summary: A life-size wooden crucifix in which Christ is shown alive and upright on the cross, eyes open and head gently inclined, wearing a long, belted, sleeved tunic (colobium) that leaves only his hands and feet bare. This photograph shows it after the restoration completed in 2025, surrounded by later ornaments, including a nimbus of about 1410 and a dove of the early 20th century. Medieval legend held that Nicodemus, who helped bury Christ, carved it and that an angel completed the face, and that it reached Lucca in 782; radiocarbon tests announced in 2020 placed the wood in the late 8th or early 9th century, making it one of the oldest surviving wooden crucifixes of the Christian West.
facts: In June 2020 the Italian National Institute for Nuclear Physics (INFN) presented radiocarbon results dating the crucifix to between the last decades of the 8th century and the beginning of the 9th — overturning the older view that it was a 12th–13th-century replacement.

According to the 'Leobinus legend', the image was found in the Holy Land by a bishop guided by a dream and arrived by a boat without sail or crew at Luni, before being brought to Lucca on an ox-cart without a driver.

It stands in an octagonal marble tempietto built for it by Matteo Civitali in 1484, and the city honours it each year with the candlelit Luminara procession on 13 September; many copies spread across Europe, among them the Volto Santo of Sansepolcro and the Imervard Cross in Brunswick.
Q1780180.notes: Radiocarbon range reported as 770–880 on en.wikipedia and as late 8th–early 9th century on it.wikipedia; the Commons photographer labels it 780–820. The crucifix was re-presented on 13 September 2025 after restoration in a space in the left aisle while its tempietto is restored. Supersedes the WGA record wga:m/master/xunk_it/xunk_it6/03cross (wrongly dated c. 1200), rejected in deep-c1-legends.json.

cur:monumental-san-raising-of-lazarus.summary: Lazarus, still wrapped in his grave-clothes, stands in the doorway of a small temple-like tomb at the top of a flight of steps, as Christ, haloed and in purple, stretches out his hand to call him forth, a disciple at his side. Unlike the catacomb paintings, Christ here commands with a gesture rather than a wand.
facts: The thirteen scenes of the north wall show Christ's miracles and teaching; in all of them he appears young and beardless, robed in imperial purple.
The Raising of Lazarus, read near the end of Lent before Holy Week, was one of the most frequently depicted miracles in Early Christian art.
The scenes were not arranged in biblical order but are thought to follow the Gospel readings of the Lenten liturgy in Theodoric's palace church.
